entries.title: How can a computer notice what is happening around it?
entries.answer: A sensor is a part that notices or measures something. On a robot it could measure how much light is coming from a direction, or notice when a wheel has turned. A computer can read the measurement as information. A program can then tell the robot to turn if it notices a dark line on the floor. The sensor makes the measurement, and the instructions decide what the robot does when that measurement changes.
facts: Sensors can measure things such as light, movement, or pressure.

questions.text: What decides how to use a measurement from a sensor?
What kinds of physical pieces can detect a change?
How does your own body notice pressure or a bump?

entries.title: How can a computer read a screen aloud?
entries.answer: A screen reader is software that tells a person about what is on a screen. It can speak the words in a menu or say the name of the button a person might press next. It can also send text to a device that forms raised braille dots. A web page is easier for a screen reader to explain when it has clear headings, named buttons, and useful descriptions for pictures. A screen reader need not speak every part at once.
facts: Some screen readers send words to a device that makes raised braille dots.

questions.text: How do people use raised dots to read words?
Why should a helpful page give meaningful pictures a description?
What assembles the online material that can be read?

entries.title: How can a computer store a sound?
entries.answer: Sound can make a microphone create a changing electrical signal. To hold a recording, a device can measure that signal again and again at very short steps in time. Each measurement is called a sample. Saving the numbers lets a player build a changing signal later. It sends that signal to a speaker. When the speaker moves air back and forth, you can hear a sound close to the one that was recorded.
facts: A recording can save many thousands of sample measurements each second.

questions.text: What sort of movement starts the sound a microphone records?
How can each sound measurement be stored as a number?
Why might a long recording need a smaller file?

entries.title: How can a computer turn a picture of a page into searchable words?
entries.answer: A picture of a page has many dots of color. Optical character recognition, or OCR, is software that looks at the shapes in the picture and guesses which letters make up its words. A search program can then look through the guessed text. Spots, smudges, and fancy print can lead to wrong guesses. When a word or date matters, a reader can check the original image to see what it really says.
facts: A scanned newspaper can show the picture of a whole page beside the text guessed by OCR.

questions.text: How does a library make page images in the first place?
How do computers agree about which code stands for each letter?
How can printed details help you understand an old photograph?

entries.title: How can a transistor work like a very small switch?
entries.answer: A transistor is a small electronic part. A signal at one point can control how much electrical current flows through another path. A computer can use this behavior to switch between states that stand for zero and one. The part does not need a moving handle like a room’s light switch. Other circuits can use transistors to help a weak signal control a stronger one, which can be useful in equipment that plays sound.
facts: An early working transistor was built at Bell Labs in 1947.

questions.text: Why do computers use two states to represent numbers and other things?
How do many transistors fit on one chip?
How does a simple on-off switch control a light?

entries.title: How could gears add numbers inside a machine?
entries.answer: In the 1800s Charles Babbage designed a machine to calculate long lists of numbers. A wheel in the machine could stand for a digit. When a wheel passed from nine back to zero, it could make the wheel beside it move one place. That worked like carrying a one in written addition. Repeating simple changes let his machine fill a table with results. Turning the mechanism supplied the motion.
facts: The Difference Engine was designed to use mechanical parts to calculate, rather than electric circuits.

questions.text: How did Ada Lovelace describe using a different machine for many kinds of tasks?
Why does a digit in one column have a different value from a digit in another?
How did a later machine make calculations with electronics?

entries.title: How could holes in paper help count people?
entries.answer: Before modern computers, clerks could put information about a person on a stiff paper card by making holes in chosen spots. A counting machine checked those spots. If a hole was there, part of the machine could make an electrical connection and add to a count. Sorting the cards made it easier to compare groups. For the 1890 United States census, the same kinds of counting steps could be run over many cards.
facts: Herman Hollerith helped develop the counting and sorting system used for that census.

questions.text: Why does the United States count the people who live there?
How can a choice between two states stand for information?
How did a later device hold information without holes?

entries.title: How do computers agree which letters to show?
entries.answer: A text program needs a shared way to know which letter or sign a stored number means. Unicode assigns a number to a letter, sign, or other text character. Different computers can use the same numbers to tell what was written. A number can describe the same letter even though different fonts draw it with different shapes. When you move text from one program to another, that agreement helps it say the same thing.
facts: Unicode can represent letters from many languages as well as math signs and emoji.

questions.text: What is an alphabet, one kind of thing Unicode can describe?
How can the computer store a number using only ones and zeros?
How can those stored numbers become part of a file?

entries.title: How do computers keep files without power?
entries.answer: A computer keeps some information in devices that are built to remember without power. They can hold drawings, recordings, and programs between uses. A hard drive stores information with magnetism on spinning surfaces. A solid-state drive uses chips instead. When you open a saved drawing, the computer reads the stored information and can place a working copy in faster memory. Changes still need to be saved if you want to find them later.
facts: Solid-state storage can keep information when the computer is switched off.

questions.text: What is different about memory used for current work?
How do computers organize saved information into named groups?
Why keep a second copy of something you do not want to lose?

entries.title: How do folders help you find files?
entries.answer: If all of your saved work were in one big pile, it could be hard to find a particular drawing. A folder lets you give a name to a group of files. It can also contain more folders. You might make one folder called School and a folder inside it called Science. The trail of folder names tells the computer and you how to get to a particular saved file. More than one folder can contain an item with the same name.
facts: A folder on a computer is also called a directory.

questions.text: What is one of the things that belongs in a folder?
Where does a computer store the contents you organize?
How can you keep a copy of a collection of files?

entries.title: How do many electronic parts fit on a single chip?
entries.answer: An integrated circuit puts many tiny electronic parts on one piece of material. The parts can include transistors and very small tracks that join them. Making the connections as part of the chip saves space. It also lets factories make many copies of the same design. One chip can do a simple job like adding numbers or a larger job like helping a computer follow the instructions for an entire program.
facts: Some of the earliest integrated circuit designs appeared in the late 1950s.

questions.text: How can a tiny part control an electrical signal?
How does a computer’s processor follow instructions?
Why did some early computers take up an entire room?

entries.title: How do programmers find and fix bugs?
entries.answer: A bug is a problem in a program. Imagine a score that goes up when the player should lose a point. A programmer can replay the same move and check what happens before and after it. This narrows the search for the instructions causing the change. Fixing the bug means finding that problem, changing what causes it, and trying the move again. A test can also help check that the fix has not broken other parts of the game.
facts: A bug can make a program give a wrong answer even when it appears to run normally.

questions.text: How can looking at each step reveal one that does not work?
What instructions can be changed when you fix a program?
What kinds of saved values might you check while tracing an error?

entries.title: How do screens mix red, green, and blue light?
entries.answer: Many screens create colors by mixing red, green, and blue light. A little spot on the screen can get a different amount of each color. If the blue part shines brightly and the other parts shine very little, the spot looks blue. Strong red and green light together can look yellow. Amounts of all three can produce pale colors or white. The method mixes light, so the result can differ from mixing red, green, and blue paint.
facts: RGB stands for red, green, and blue.

questions.text: What makes mixtures of colored light possible?
How do colored points fit together to make an image?
How does your eye take in the light a screen makes?

entries.title: How does a computer mouse tell which way it moved?
entries.answer: An optical mouse shines light onto the surface beneath it. A tiny sensor makes images of that small patch again and again. A chip compares the images to see which way little marks and shadows have shifted. It sends the change to the computer, which moves the pointer. A surface with a visible pattern often gives the mouse more clues than smooth, clear glass.
facts: An optical mouse can notice movement even when your hand slides it only a short way.

questions.text: How can a smoke alarm make use of light hitting a sensor?
Why does a bright surface sometimes send light straight back?
What does a sensor do when a car stops over a traffic detector?

entries.title: How does a database help find a record?
entries.answer: A database is an organized store of information that a program can look through. A class library’s database might store one record for every book. The record could include a title and who wrote it. A question like “Which books were written by this person?” asks the database to look for records with a certain name. Keeping the same kinds of details together helps a program return a useful list without reading a shelf of book covers.
facts: A library catalog is one way people search a stored collection of records.

questions.text: How can a grid help people organize some smaller collections?
Why do a search engine’s records let it find pages quickly?
Why might a store link a scanned number to a saved record?

entries.title: How does a router pass a message between networks?
entries.answer: A router joins networks and helps information travel between them. When a packet comes in, router equipment looks at where it is headed. It uses that information to send the packet to a useful next place. Many routers could handle the same packet on a long trip. Think of a station that sorts mail toward different towns. The station does not have to take each note all the way across the country by itself.
facts: A box at home can combine a router with a Wi-Fi access point.

questions.text: What smaller parts does a router send along?
Why do smaller local networks need ways to link together?
How can a device reach a nearby network without plugging in?

entries.title: How does a search engine find pages?
entries.answer: A search engine can find pages ahead of time and build a list of clues about them. That list is often called an index. When you type a question, the program can look through its index quickly. It tries to show pages that seem useful for the words you typed. The list is not a list of everything on the Web, and the first result is not always the best answer. Reading a trustworthy page still matters.
facts: A new page may take time to appear in a search list.

questions.text: What program opens a result after you choose it?
Where do many of the linked pages live?
What does a result need so the browser can open the page?

entries.title: How does a web address tell a browser what to open?
entries.answer: A web address is often called a URL. It can name a site and say which thing you want there. The name of the site helps the browser find where to send its request. Another part can describe a page or file within the site. A piece at the end can point to a spot in a page you are opening. Look at the site name before you follow a link, because the words you see on a button need not be the place it goes.
facts: The piece after a # can point to a spot within a page.

questions.text: Which program can use the address to ask for materials?
Who answers requests for things at those addresses?
How can pages point to each other with these addresses?

entries.title: How does computer memory hold what you are using?
entries.answer: Think of your desk while you work. You may set out just the books and papers you need right now. A computer has a work area called RAM. It holds instructions and a copy of some information that programs are using. The processor can reach that space quickly. If you turn the computer off, most kinds of RAM forget what they held. Saving moves a lasting copy to a different part of the machine.
facts: Most ordinary RAM loses its contents when it no longer has power.

questions.text: Where can you put a file to keep it after turning off the machine?
What part asks the working memory for an instruction?
What helps several apps share the machine’s memory?

entries.title: How does Wi-Fi connect a device without a cable?
entries.answer: Wi-Fi is one way for a device to join a nearby network. Instead of a cable to the device, it uses radio signals. An access point nearby can send and receive those signals, so you may be able to use a laptop in different parts of a room. Sometimes that little network connects to the internet through other equipment. Sometimes it does not. Seeing the Wi-Fi symbol means there is a wireless connection, rather than a promise that every website will work.
facts: A device can have a Wi-Fi connection to a nearby network that cannot reach the internet.

questions.text: What is the local connection doing even before the internet is involved?
What can pass a small message from one network toward another?
How does a nearby network reach faraway ones?

entries.title: Is the Web the same as the internet?
entries.answer: The Web is a huge collection of pages and other things that can get linked together. A browser gets a page from a place that can send it and lets you follow a link to another page. The internet is the bigger network that carries the pieces of pages between computers. Other activities also use the internet. Think of the internet as the routes a letter can travel, and the Web as a collection of notes with pointers between them.
facts: A link in a web page can lead to another page on a different site.

questions.text: What wider network carries the parts of web pages?
What kinds of programs can show pages from the Web?
How does a link refer to a particular place on the Web?

entries.title: What are pixels in a picture?
entries.answer: Many pictures on a computer are made of rows and columns of small spots called pixels. One part of the picture can contain darker pixels, while another contains lighter ones. Your eyes see the spots together as a shape or scene. If you zoom in enough, the spots may look like square blocks. Each block shows one saved part of the image, a little like a piece in a mosaic. Other kinds of pictures can describe lines and shapes instead.
facts: A drawing that stores every pixel is one kind of bitmap image.

questions.text: What happens when an image can store more pixels across the same scene?
How can one colored picture point store a mixture of three colors?
What other sort of digital picture describes shapes instead of a grid?

entries.title: What did Ada Lovelace imagine a calculating machine could do?
entries.answer: Ada Lovelace wrote about a design for a machine called the Analytical Engine. She explained a way to give it steps for calculating a series of numbers. She also thought about what a machine might do if its numbers stood for things besides amounts, such as parts of music. The whole machine was never finished in her lifetime. Her notes showed that the way instructions are arranged matters as much as the machine that follows them.
facts: Lovelace’s notes about Charles Babbage’s design appeared in 1843.

questions.text: How can moving wheels store and add digits?
How does an algorithm explain steps in order?
How can numbers stand for information inside a modern computer?

entries.title: What do captions do in a video?
entries.answer: Captions put words on a video near the time of the sound they explain. They can tell you what someone says and can also note important sounds. For instance, they may tell you when someone knocks at a door just before a character turns around. Captions are useful for people who cannot hear the sound or are in a place where they cannot turn it up. Reading a caption can let you follow the moment the sound happens.
facts: Captions can label an important sound even when nobody is speaking.

questions.text: How can text describe a part of a page you see rather than hear?
What does a recording keep about the sound itself?
How can a device turn written words into sound?

entries.title: What does a computer processor do?
entries.answer: A processor is a chip that follows many simple instructions very quickly. One instruction might ask it to add two numbers. Another might tell it to compare them or get a piece of information from memory. A long series of such acts can help a game decide whether two shapes touched. Usually more than one part of the machine helps with a large job. The processor leads much of the step-by-step work your programs ask for.
facts: CPU is short for central processing unit.

questions.text: Where does a processor find much of what it is currently using?
Where do the work instructions come from?
Why are the instructions stored using strings of ones and zeros?

entries.title: What does a QR code do?
entries.answer: A QR code is a kind of barcode with light and dark areas set out in a square. A camera and an app can look at the pattern and turn it into information. Some QR codes store a web address so you do not have to type it, while others store short pieces of text. The code is just a way of recording the information. It cannot promise that the page it points to is the one you expected.
facts: A QR code can store a web address, but a code can contain other kinds of information too.

questions.text: How does a scanner use a row of marks on a package?
What is the kind of address a QR code can send to a browser?
Why pause before entering your details on an unfamiliar page?

entries.title: What does a variable do in a program?
entries.answer: A variable gives a program a name it can use when it needs a particular bit of information. A simple game might have a variable called score. At first the score could be zero. When your player gathers a star, the game could use the old number to work out the new one. Giving the number a name helps the game use it again. Variables can also refer to things other than numbers, such as a player’s name.
facts: The number a variable refers to can change as a program runs.

questions.text: How might you check whether the value of a score is changing correctly?
How can a named bit of code use a value it is given?
Why can a sequence of steps keep track of a running total?

entries.title: What does a web browser do?
entries.answer: A browser is a program for opening and showing web pages. It uses the address you give it to ask another computer for material. The reply may include writing, pictures, and instructions for showing those pieces together. The browser lays them out on your screen. When you click a link, it can ask for something else. A search engine can be one site you visit using a browser, rather than the program that displays every site.
facts: A browser can fetch materials requested by an address or by a link on a page.

questions.text: Where can a browser get a page from?
How is a search engine different from the browser that shows it?
What address can you give to a browser to ask for a page?

entries.title: What does a web server do?
entries.answer: A web server is equipment and software that can answer a request for web content. Suppose your browser asks for a school’s lunch menu. A server might find a saved menu file and send its contents back. Another kind of request could make a server build a reply from information it holds. Your browser still decides how to show what it receives. Both sides follow shared rules so the request and the reply make sense.
facts: A server can send files or can make a new reply to a particular request.

questions.text: What asks for the page and shows you the reply?
How does a request tell the server which thing to send?
How can a big reply travel through shared connections?

entries.title: What does compressing a computer file do?
entries.answer: Computer files can take up less room if the information is stored in a shorter form. For example, a long string of twenty red spots might be stored as one note saying to draw twenty in a row. The program has to understand that kind of note when it opens the file. Some real kinds of compression use patterns like repetition. Others can make it even smaller by dropping details that many people will hardly notice.
facts: Some kinds of compression let a program restore every bit in the original file.

questions.text: When is it possible to get back exactly what you started with?
Why can smaller files be useful when storage is limited?
Where could a picture contain repeated blocks of color?

entries.title: What does the resolution of a picture mean?
entries.answer: One way to describe a digital picture’s resolution is to count how many pixels it has across and down. A larger count can hold smaller details when the picture was captured with those details in it. If you only stretch an old small picture to fill a bigger grid, the new squares do not magically reveal shapes the old file missed. They are guessed from the neighboring colors. That is why a small blurry picture can still be blurry when it fills a screen.
facts: A picture 200 pixels wide and 100 pixels tall has 20,000 pixel positions.

questions.text: What is each little position in the grid called?
Why can a shape drawing scale without a fixed grid of stored colors?
How can a large picture file take up less room?

entries.title: What extra information can a file keep about itself?
entries.answer: A digital file can include details about the information it holds. A picture could keep a description of its size or the date it was made. Those details are called metadata. A library or a computer can use these clues to find particular material without looking at every picture first. One file may have different details from the next. When you send a photo to someone else, the material that travels may include details besides the picture you can see on the screen.
facts: A file’s properties may describe its type or when it was last changed.

questions.text: What is the main information inside a named file?
What information makes up the actual picture you see?
What kinds of extra clues can matter when you send a photo?

entries.title: What is a computer network?
entries.answer: A computer network links devices so they can send information to each other. For instance, a computer and a printer can share a link. The computer can send the information needed to make a page on paper. Other networks join many computers that share things with each other. They need a set of agreed ways to send and receive messages, just as people agree when to speak and listen during a conversation.
facts: Devices can share information over wires or through radio signals.

questions.text: How do many networks join into the largest network we use?
How does a device join a nearby network without a wire?
How can a message move in small groups of data?

entries.title: What is a file on a computer?
entries.answer: A file is a named group of stored information. A picture file may contain colors in a grid. Another file may hold the words in a story or the measurements from a recording. When you open the file, a program reads it in a way that fits what is in it. Giving the file a useful name helps you find it later. Saving a file and leaving a drawing open for now are different actions.
facts: A file can hold a picture, a story, a recording, or numbers.

questions.text: How can you keep related files together?
What can the end of a file name tell you?
Where does the computer keep a file after it is saved?

entries.title: What is an algorithm?
entries.answer: An algorithm is a set of steps for solving a problem or doing a job. Imagine looking for your name in a list that is sorted from A to Z. One plan is to start at the top and read each name in order. Another is to start near the middle and decide which half to keep looking in. Both can find your name, but the second plan can save time on a long sorted list. Computers can follow algorithms when each step is clear enough for them to carry it out.

sections.heading: A useful rule can have a condition
sections.text: If the name at the middle comes before yours, look in the later half. If it comes after yours, look in the earlier half.

facts: An algorithm can be followed by a person as well as by a computer.
Fast ways of looking through a sorted list depend on the list being in order.

questions.text: How does a computer represent information while it works?
How can one short set of steps help you count a rectangle’s tiles?
What clues should a person check before following a message’s instructions?

entries.title: What is an operating system?
entries.answer: An operating system is a set of programs that helps a computer run. It can give apps a way to open files, read keys, play sounds, or draw on the screen. It also keeps track of things that more than one app may need, such as the processor and memory. A game can ask the operating system to play a sound instead of having to know how each kind of speaker works.
facts: Phones and tablets also use operating systems.

questions.text: What kinds of instructions can run as apps?
What is the working space that apps need to share?
What does the operating system help store and open?

entries.title: What is computer hardware?
entries.answer: A screen, a keyboard, and the pieces inside a laptop are all hardware. Hardware is the physical part of a computer. Some pieces let you send in information, as when you press a key. Others can show or play a result. The parts deep inside do work such as following instructions or storing an image. Computers come in many shapes, but they need pieces built to carry out jobs their programs ask for.
facts: A phone and a desktop computer both contain processors and memory.

questions.text: What tells these physical parts what to do?
What part holds the information being worked on right now?
What parts can keep a file when the power is off?

entries.title: What is software?
entries.answer: If you can use one tablet to draw and then play a game, it is because different software runs on the same equipment. Software includes instructions that the computer can follow. A drawing app tells it how to react when you drag a finger, while a music app tells it how to play sound. Other software helps those apps talk to the parts inside. New instructions can change what a computer does without replacing the physical machine.
facts: Programs can turn the same physical device into a drawing tool, a music player, or a game.

questions.text: What is the physical equipment that runs the program?
What program helps other programs share the machine?
How do clear steps help you describe what a program should do?

entries.title: What is the difference between lossy and lossless files?
entries.answer: If you make a story file smaller and later want every letter back, the method must save enough information to rebuild the whole thing. That is lossless compression. Lossy compression can shrink a picture by keeping a close version of part of it and skipping some fine detail. That can be useful if exact detail matters less than file size. You cannot count on the missing detail to come back when the small file opens.
facts: Plain text usually needs to be recovered exactly when a compressed file opens.

questions.text: How can saving repeated patterns make a file smaller?
What do some formats save about a changing sound?
What clue might help you tell what sort of picture file you have?

entries.title: What is the internet?
entries.answer: The internet is a system that links many computer networks. Your device can send information to a nearby network, which has ways to reach others. That lets a message travel to a device far away even though there is no single wire joining the two. Devices use agreed rules to pass information along. Web pages are one thing people send this way. Messages, calls, and some multiplayer games also use the internet.
facts: The internet carries more than web pages. It can also carry messages and game information.

questions.text: Which collection of pages uses the internet to reach readers?
What sends packets toward the network they need?
How can a local wireless connection give a device access to somewhere farther away?

entries.title: Why can a box appear in place of a letter on a screen?
entries.answer: A computer can know which letter was typed and still lack a shape to draw it on the screen. The file stores a number code for the letter. The computer looks in a font, which is a set of shapes for it to draw. If it cannot find a shape in any font it can use, it might draw a little box instead. With a different font, the same text may show the letter correctly.
facts: A missing-letter box can appear even when the text file still contains the correct character code.

questions.text: How do computers agree which code stands for each letter?
Why do two scripts sometimes share a letter shape but not a sound?
How can a computer guess what letters appear in an image?

entries.title: Why can a vector picture grow without getting blocky?
entries.answer: A vector picture can describe a shape by saying where its edges and curves go. A drawing of a blue circle can be saved as the circle’s center, its size, and its color. To make the drawing bigger, a program redraws those shapes at a new size. It does not have to stretch a fixed set of color spots from the original. This works well for a sign or a chart with clean edges. A photograph is usually stored differently.
facts: SVG is one way to store a vector image.

questions.text: How can another kind of picture store a color at each spot?
Why can a small grid of pixels look blurry after you enlarge it?
What filename-ending clue might tell you that a file is a vector image?

entries.title: Why do computers send messages in little packets?
entries.answer: A long message can share a busy route more easily if it travels as little pieces called packets. Think of mailing a long story as a series of postcards. A packet carries some of the message and information that helps move it to its destination. Depending on the rules in use, the receiving device can take the pieces and make a complete message. Smaller pieces make it possible for many conversations to share busy routes.
facts: Packet information can help devices send and put pieces of a message where they belong.

questions.text: How do packets get passed between networks?
What larger system lets packets reach faraway computers?
How can a browser use those pieces to open something you requested?

entries.title: Why do computers use 0s and 1s?
entries.answer: A computer can store a tiny piece of information in one of two states. We give those states the names 0 and 1. One such choice is called a bit. Put bits together and you can make patterns. A set of agreed rules can tell a computer which pattern stands for a letter, a number, or a color. Binary numbers use only 0 and 1. Their places count in ones, twos, fours, eights, and so on, each place worth twice as much as the one to its right.

sections.heading: Read 101 in binary
sections.text: Start at the right. There is one 1, no 2s, and one 4. Add them together and you get 5.

facts: One byte is eight bits.
Three bits can make eight different patterns.

questions.text: What decides how a computer works with these patterns?
How can electricity travel through a path that opens and closes?
What is another way numbers can show amounts?

entries.title: Why do people organize information in a spreadsheet?
entries.answer: A spreadsheet is a table of little spaces arranged in rows and columns. One column could name each fruit your class counts, and another could hold how many you saw. Each small space can keep its own number, name, or calculation. A grid lets you compare like things in neighboring rows or add a group of numbers together. If the class counts more apples, changing their number in one place can help a spreadsheet update a total elsewhere.
facts: Squares in a spreadsheet are often named using a column letter and a row number.

questions.text: What general name describes the steps that can tell a computer to add a group of cells?
What other tool helps keep and search large sets of records?
How can you arrange the rows in an order that helps you find something?

entries.title: Why do programs use functions?
entries.answer: A program can give a name to a group of steps it may use again. One name for that group is a function. A drawing program could have a function that draws a star. Each time the program calls it, the function follows the steps to make one. It could also take a position or color as extra information. Keeping the star-drawing steps in one place makes it easier to change how all the stars look.
facts: Several parts of a program can call the same function.

questions.text: How can a function receive information that changes?
How can you plan the steps a function has to follow?
Why might fixing one function repair several things at once?

entries.title: Why do some filenames end in .jpg or .txt?
entries.answer: The end of a filename after a dot often tells you what kind of file it is. For example, .jpg commonly names one kind of picture file, and .txt often names plain text. The ending is called a file extension. Your device may use that clue to choose a program to open it. Changing the ending alone does not rearrange the bits into a new kind of picture. To switch the type, you usually need a program that can read the old one and save the new one.
facts: A different extension does not by itself change the information inside a file.

entries.title: Why keep a backup copy of a file?
entries.answer: A backup is an extra copy that helps you get a file back if something happens to the one you use. If a drawing is saved in one place and both your computer and the drawing disappear, you have no second copy there. A copy stored somewhere else can protect a drawing or photo from being lost along with that device. Families can decide together what is worth backing up and check that they can read the backup.
facts: A backup is useful only if it still contains a copy you can get back.

entries.title: Why might a web page load faster the second time?
entries.answer: The first time a browser shows a page, it may ask for the text, pictures, and other parts separately. It can keep copies of some of those parts in a space called a cache. If you return later and the copies are still useful, it can read them again instead of asking for everything to travel over the network. Sometimes it must check for a newer copy. Keeping a reusable copy can make a return visit to the same page faster.
facts: A cache can be temporary and may need to check for a newer version.

entries.title: Why was an old floppy disk called floppy?
entries.answer: An early floppy disk held a thin, flexible circle inside a sleeve. A drive spun the disk and moved a small part over its surface to read or write patterns of magnetism. People could take the disk out and move the information to another computer. Some later floppy disks had hard outer cases, but the disk hidden inside was still flexible. A floppy disk could carry only a small amount compared with many drives today.
facts: IBM used a floppy disk to load computer data in 1971.

entries.title: Why was ENIAC so much bigger than a modern computer?
entries.answer: ENIAC was an early electronic computer. Its thousands of vacuum tubes helped it switch electrical signals and make calculations quickly. Each tube took up space, and the machine needed many wires and panels to connect them. People set up many early jobs by changing switches and making cable connections. A modern chip puts far more tiny electronic parts in much less space, so a powerful computer can fit in your pocket.
facts: ENIAC filled a large room at the University of Pennsylvania.

entries.title: Why would an online picture have a text description?
entries.answer: A page can give a picture a short description called alt text. A screen reader can speak those words so someone can understand the part the picture plays even when they cannot see it. The useful words may depend on the rest of the page. If a picture is a button, saying what the button does is often more helpful than naming its colors. A picture of a changing graph might need its most important message explained in words.
facts: Good text for a picture depends on what the picture is doing on that page.
